title: Rosalind and the Winter
premise: Edmund Ravensworth, a hardened pest controller and committed skeptic, is hired to investigate strange frost patterns and sleep disturbances at Hollowmere House, where a family claims something with fingerprints has been visiting them in the night. As he sets up recording equipment to debunk the haunting, the tapes capture a second voice answering questions no one asked aloud—a voice that knows Edmund's own buried past. The entity was invited in generations ago by a Ravensworth ancestor, and it has been waiting for a family member to return so it can claim a body and a name. Edmund must survive one final night in the house, resisting the thing's offers of belonging and power, until sunrise breaks the frost's hold—though he escapes only by accepting that the 'family' he finds there, the frightened householders who refuse to abandon him, matter more than the bloodline that doomed him.
about_author: Coral Lockridge is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing estate records in northern England, where she collected more ghost stories than documents. She writes horror about skeptical people forced to take the impossible seriously.

chapters.title: The Callout
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Edmund. A routine pest-control call turns strange: the client insists the problem is 'something with fingerprints' pressing through frosted windows. Edmund takes the job for the money, mocking the superstition. Emotional beat: his weary certainty that every haunting is rats, drafts, or grief.

chapters.title: Hollowmere House
chapters.summary: Edmund arrives at the decaying manor and meets the Ashcombe family—worn mother Marion, sharp-eyed teen daughter Ivy, and the silent youngest, Toby, who hasn't slept properly in weeks. The house is cold in ways the boiler can't explain. Beat: unease seeded by small wrong details.

chapters.title: Fingerprints
chapters.summary: Edmund inspects the windows and finds handprints pressed into interior frost—small, child-sized, five-fingered, but with too many joints. He photographs them and tells himself condensation. Beat: the first crack in his skepticism, quickly plastered over.

chapters.title: Equipment
chapters.summary: Edmund sets up audio recorders and a camera in Toby's room, planning to catch a draught or a hoax. Ivy watches him with contempt, calling him another adult who won't listen. Beat: friction establishing found-family stakes; Ivy becomes his reluctant ally.

chapters.title: First Night
chapters.summary: Edmund stays overnight in the guest room, dozing in a chair. At 3:11 a.m. the temperature plummets; frost blooms across the inside of the glass in fern patterns. Nothing else happens—but his recorder picks up forty minutes of breathing. Beat: dread without proof.

chapters.title: The Tapes
chapters.summary: Reviewing footage, Edmund hears a second voice on the recording—low, patient, answering questions. The problem: no one in the room asked anything aloud. The voice says his name. Beat: skepticism collapses into obsession; he replays it until dawn.

chapters.title: What It Knows
chapters.summary: The voice on subsequent recordings begins addressing Edmund directly, reciting details of his childhood in care, his mother's abandonment, his refusal of his own surname for years. POV shifts briefly to Ivy, who catches him listening and doesn't mock him. Beat: identity theme ignites.

chapters.title: Marion's Confession
chapters.summary: Marion admits the family moved in knowing the house's reputation; the previous owners left a box of papers in the cellar. She stayed because they had nowhere else. Beat: desperation and complicity—the family invited Edmund into a place they half-believed was hungry.

chapters.title: The Cellar Box
chapters.summary: Edmund and Ivy find deeds, letters, and a portrait: a Ravensworth ancestor, Josiah, who 'contracted' with something during a famine winter to save his household. The price deferred, not paid. Beat: Edmund realizes the entity isn't haunting the house—it's waiting for him.

chapters.title: It Speaks
chapters.summary: That night the voice comes through the recorder live, conversational, offering Edmund what he's always wanted: a name, a lineage, a place that was always his. It calls itself family. Beat: temptation rendered genuinely warm, which makes it worse.

chapters.title: Ivy's Theory
chapters.summary: Ivy, who has researched obsessively, lays out the pattern: the entity strengthens each winter, needs a consenting Ravensworth, and has been grooming Edmund through the tapes. She proposes they destroy the recordings. Beat: alliance solidifies into genuine trust—found family taking shape.

chapters.title: Toby
chapters.summary: The youngest child speaks for the first time in weeks, describing 'the cold uncle' who tucks him in and asks him to open the door. Edmund realizes the entity has been working on the weakest member as leverage. Beat: protective fury; stakes become visceral.

chapters.title: Cutting the Lines
chapters.summary: Edmund tries to sever contact: burns the tapes, boards the cellar, plans to leave. But frost handprints appear on his car windshield from the inside, and the radio plays his mother's lullaby. Beat: the trap closing; escape revealed as illusion.

chapters.title: Josiah's Letters
chapters.summary: Deciphering Josiah's final letter, Edmund learns the terms: the entity may be refused, but only by a Ravensworth who chooses to stay of free will through one full winter night without accepting any gift offered. Refusal by flight passes the debt to the next generation. Beat: the rules of the climax established.

chapters.title: The Offer Made Plain
chapters.summary: The entity drops pretense, appearing in frost-form at the foot of Edmund's bed: it can restore his name, erase his childhood, make him heir to everything—including the house, warm forever. All it wants is his yes. Beat: power and its corruption distilled into a single seductive sentence.

chapters.title: Marion Breaks
chapters.summary: Marion, exhausted and terrified for Toby, begs Edmund to just say yes and end it—let the entity have him if it spares her children. The found family fractures under fear. Beat: betrayal and its immediate regret; lowest relational point.

chapters.title: The Long Night Begins
chapters.summary: Winter solstice. Edmund sends the family away against their protests—Ivy refuses, staying hidden upstairs—and settles in for the night of refusal. The entity begins its campaign: warmth, memory, guilt, each gift declined. Beat: quiet, controlled dread; the siege starts.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Midnight hours. The entity shows Edmund the truth: Josiah didn't summon it—it answered a starving child's prayer, and every generation since has fed it just enough hope to keep it bound. It is lonely, and it lies. Beat: pity complicating horror; Edmund nearly wavers.

chapters.title: Ivy's Door
chapters.summary: Near dawn, the entity abandons gifts and takes hostages of a sort: it seals the house, freezes the doors, and goes for Ivy and Toby. Edmund must choose between holding silence and screaming his consent to save them. Beat: climax pressure at maximum.

chapters.title: Refusal
chapters.summary: Edmund refuses—not with silence but with declaration: he wants none of it, not the name, not the house, not the power, and he will not trade the children for himself. The frost shatters inward. Sunrise hits the windows. Beat: cathartic climax; identity claimed on his own terms.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: The house thaws. The Ashcombes return; Marion apologizes; Ivy and Edmund share tea amid broken glass and melting frost. The recordings are gone, but Edmund keeps one photograph of the handprints—as evidence, or maybe as thanks. Beat: tender, exhausted relief.

chapters.title: Spring at Hollowmere
chapters.summary: Weeks later, Edmund has taken a room at Hollowmere while repairs proceed—staying not because of the debt but because he was asked. Toby sleeps through the night. On the last page, a single new fern of frost appears on a window, and Edmund simply closes the curtain. Beat: resolution with an earned, ambiguous exhale.
